question: Is Paul a reliable source for what Jesus taught?
finding: Paul never met the living Jesus, and he grounds the authority of his gospel in private revelation rather than in anything handed to him by the men who did: "not of man, neither was I taught it." He wrote the only surviving body of Christian theology that almost never quotes Jesus. He reversed in writing a ruling James had given with him in the room, and the Jewish-Christian communities with direct lineage to that church named him an opponent. This is not a claim about his character; nothing here requires him to be a fraud. The claim is structural: Paul's gospel has a different source and a different content from the teaching of Jesus. He is a primary source for Paul's theology, and not a source for what Jesus taught.
oneLiners: Paul told us himself what his gospel rested on: "not of man, neither was I taught it." That's the quote, in his own letter.
Thirteen books, two thousand verses, and he quotes Jesus about twice. If you want the teaching, you're reading the wrong author.
He met Peter for fifteen days and came back with a creed, not a Sermon on the Mount.
Luther couldn't harmonize Paul and James either. He just decided James had to go.
doNotSay: "Paul fails the Acts 1:21-22 test for apostleship." That's the criterion for filling Judas's seat; Barnabas, James and Junia are called apostles too. We're not arguing he wasn't an apostle, only that he isn't an eyewitness source for the teaching.
"Paul lied." The three conversion narratives in Acts are evidence about Luke's method, not Paul's honesty.
"Deuteronomy 18:22 convicts him." That's a character argument and we don't need one. The structural point is enough.

Quoting Acts where it suits us and dismissing it where it doesn't. State the rule up front: Acts is weighted where it embarrasses its own harmonizing agenda; where Acts and the letters conflict, the letters win.

sources.note: He locates his gospel's authority in revelation, not in transmission from the eyewitnesses. Read on: "neither went I up to Jerusalem to them which were apostles before me" (1:17).

Of the Jerusalem pillars. Every clause of the paragraph minimizes dependence: not immediately, not to the apostles, three years later, fifteen days, only James, and then "added nothing." That is his claim, not ours.

The one place he unambiguously transmits received material is a creed and an appearance list, not teaching. Across the undisputed letters he cites a saying of Jesus about twice: divorce (1 Cor 7:10-11) and support for preachers (1 Cor 9:14), plus the Supper words, which he credits "of the Lord" (11:23). No parables, no Sermon on the Mount, no Matthew 25.

sources.tier: Acts · weighted where it embarrasses its own agenda
sources.note: James presides and decides; Paul does not overrule him in the room. Luke has no motive to invent Jerusalem constraining Paul.

sources.note: Communities claiming descent from the Jerusalem church preserved a tradition in which Peter's authority and a visionary apostle's authority were in direct conflict. Cited for that, not as eyewitness history. See also Homilies 17.19.

sources.edition: Rev. Thomas Smith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886), from Rufinus's Latin, public domain
sources.note: "That enemy" throws James from the Temple steps, then takes a commission from Caiaphas to Damascus (1.71). Unnamed, but the commission is Saul's in Acts 9. Specialists date this source to about 150-200: a counter-history to Acts from the James side, not eyewitness history.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 12
sources.edition: Lambdin, in Robinson (ed.), The Nag Hammadi Library
sources.note: Jesus appointing James. Cite as an independent sayings tradition, not a 50s-CE text; James's primacy stands on Acts 15, Galatians 2, Hegesippus and Josephus without it.

sources.phrase: went up to Jerusalem to see Peter
sources.note: "He spent fifteen days with Peter and met James. That destroys your premise." Correct, and we raise it ourselves. The verb is historēsai, to make inquiry. The paragraph's every clause minimizes what he owed the visit, and the letters show what didn't come back from it: Jesus's sayings.

"The pillars accepted him." Paul's own account of a meeting whose outcome he then overrode in practice. Acts 21:20-25 has Jerusalem still anxious about him a decade later, asking him to prove publicly that he isn't teaching Jews to abandon Moses.

"Peter personally endorses him." The most widely doubted book in the New Testament; conservative scholars defend Petrine authorship, critical scholars date it late. On anyone's dating, the passage concedes Paul's letters contain "things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest."

sources.title: Dunn, Wright, Sanders on "works of the law"
sources.note: "Works of the law means Jewish boundary markers, not good deeds; the contradiction dissolves." The strongest scholarly objection, and the evidence for it is partly ours (4QMMT). Three answers: it is a reading of Paul, not a source for Paul; it makes the break with James sharper, not softer; and it doesn't reach Jesus's own words.

sources.phrase: justified by faith without the deeds of the law
sources.note: The verse James 2:24 answers. Same verb (dikaioō), same patriarch (Abraham: Romans 4:2 against James 2:21), opposite verdicts.

sources.phrase: the doers of the law shall be justified
sources.note: Paul can sound like James. Some of the tension is inside Paul, which is the point: his system needs harmonizing, and Jesus's answer doesn't.

sources.title: 4QMMT, "some of the works of the Torah"

sources.note: The documented pre-Christian referent of "works of the law": a halakhic list, not a statement about human morality. Our own file says so; we don't argue against it.
